title: Sensitive information types: how does Purview recognise sensitive data?
summary: The sensitive information type definitions, limits, licensing statements and control calls are supported by Microsoft documentation. The DLP navigation needs its omitted headings and scope-selection step restored, and two supporting Microsoft pages should be added to the sources.

claims.claim: SITs are pattern-based classifiers in Microsoft Purview.
claims.quote: Sensitive information types (SITs) are pattern-based classifiers.

claims.claim: SITs detect social security numbers.
claims.quote: They detect sensitive information like social security, credit card, or bank account numbers to identify sensitive items

claims.claim: SITs detect credit card numbers.
claims.quote: They detect sensitive information like social security, credit card, or bank account numbers to identify sensitive items

claims.claim: SITs detect bank account numbers.

claims.quote: Argentina national identity (DNI) number

claims.where: summary; What it is: Where SITs are used; Why it matters; What to check
claims.claim: Each SIT in a DLP rule has a confidence level that the administrator can choose.
claims.quote: SITs have a predefined confidence level which you can alter if needed.

claims.where: What it is: Where SITs are used; Why it matters; What to check
claims.claim: Each SIT in a DLP rule has an instance count condition.
claims.quote: For a scanned item to satisfy the rule criteria, the number of unique instances of a SIT in any single item must fall between the min and max values. This is called the Instance count.

claims.claim: A rule using a SIT determines whether to block, rather than the SIT itself.
claims.quote: DLP rules define sensitive information to be protected and the actions to take on rule matches.

claims.claim: Labeling rules use SIT conditions to determine whether to apply a label.
claims.quote: So you can, for example, automatically apply a Highly Confidential label to any content that contains customers' personal information, such as credit card numbers, social security numbers, or passport numbers:

claims.claim: Retention labeling policies determine retention actions for content matching SIT conditions.
claims.quote: Automatically apply a retention label to retain or delete content

claims.claim: DLP rules determine whether a match generates an alert.
claims.quote: Make sure the Send an alert to admins when a rule match occurs toggle is set to On.

claims.claim: The same SIT can produce different detection results in Exchange, SharePoint and OneDrive, and Endpoint DLP.
claims.quote: The same sensitive information type can produce different results depending on where content is evaluated—for example, email in transit (Exchange), files at rest (SharePoint and OneDrive), and files on managed devices (Endpoint DLP).

claims.where: Why it matters; Risks and limits: Endpoint DLP
claims.claim: Endpoint DLP classifies files against every SIT in the tenant, including unused custom SITs.
claims.quote: Endpoint DLP classifies files based on all sensitive information types available in the tenant, including custom sensitive information types, regardless of their utilization in any DLP policies.

claims.where: Why it matters; Risks and limits: Endpoint DLP
claims.claim: Poorly tuned SITs can cause excessive Endpoint DLP classification traffic.
claims.quote: This can cause excessive classification traffic if the sensitive information types aren't well tuned and end up matching many files.

claims.where: Risks and limits: Custom regular expressions are restricted
claims.claim: Custom SIT regex patterns must not use positional anchors such as ^ and $.

claims.claim: Multiple top-level capturing groups are blocked during custom SIT regex validation.
claims.quote: Multiple capturing groups separated by | at the top level are not supported and are blocked during validation.

claims.claim: Using a bundled named entity SIT in an endpoint DLP policy requires Advanced classification scanning and protection.
claims.quote: You must enable Advanced classification scanning and protection if you want to use a bundled SIT in an endpoint DLP policy. This requirement is specific to the combination of bundled SITS and endpoint DLP policies.

claims.where: Risks and limits: Deleting a SIT in use
claims.claim: DLP policies and Exchange mail flow rules can reference custom SITs, and references should be checked before removal.
claims.quote: Before your remove a custom sensitive information type, verify that no DLP policies or Exchange mail flow rules (also known as transport rules) still reference the sensitive information type.

claims.claim: Custom SIT creation is reached in Microsoft Purview at Information Protection > Classifiers > Sensitive info types > Create sensitive info type.
claims.quote: In the Microsoft Purview portal, navigate to Information Protection > Classifiers > Sensitive info types and choose Create sensitive info type.

claims.claim: New-DlpSensitiveInformationTypeRulePackage -FileData ([System.IO.File]::ReadAllBytes('<path to Unicode XML file>')) imports a custom SIT rule package.
claims.quote: New-DlpSensitiveInformationTypeRulePackage -FileData ([System.IO.File]::ReadAllBytes('C:\My Documents\External Sensitive Info Type Rule Collection.xml'))

claims.where: controls[0].note; Governance controls: first table row
claims.claim: To copy a SIT, select it under Sensitive info types and choose Copy on its overview page.
claims.quote: The overview page for the sensitive information type opens. Choose Copy.

claims.where: controls[0].note; Governance controls: first table row
claims.claim: A SIT with 10 text processors cannot be copied directly in the UI and must be copied using PowerShell.
claims.quote: When you have 10 text processors or restricted text processors, such as keyword lists, regex, keyword dictionaries, or functions, you won't be able to copy the SIT from the UI directly. Instead, you need to use PowerShell for this task.

claims.where: controls[0].note; Governance controls: first table row
claims.claim: A SIT with restricted text processors cannot be copied directly in the UI and must be copied using PowerShell.
claims.quote: When you have 10 text processors or restricted text processors, such as keyword lists, regex, keyword dictionaries, or functions, you won't be able to copy the SIT from the UI directly. Instead, you need to use PowerShell for this task.

claims.claim: PowerShell custom SIT creation imports an XML rule package saved with Unicode encoding.
claims.quote: Save it as an .xml file with Unicode encoding.

claims.claim: The printed Purview DLP policy creation route reaches a rule's Content contains > Add > Sensitive info types control.
claims.quote: Under Conditions, select Add condition > Content contains > Add > Sensitive info types.
claims.fix: Set controls[1].ui.path and the matching table path to 'Data loss prevention > Policies > Create policy > Enterprise applications & devices > Categories > Custom > Regulations > Custom policy > Admin units > locations > Define policy settings > Create or customize advanced DLP rules > + Create rule > Conditions > Add condition > Content contains > Add > Sensitive info types'. Here 'locations' is the policy-scope selection step. These omitted headings and scope choices are on https://learn.microsoft.com/purview/dlp-create-policy-spo-odb-quarantine; the existing selectable labels are correct and in order.

claims.claim: New-DlpComplianceRule -Name <rule name> -Policy <policy name> -ContentContainsSensitiveInformation <hashtable> creates a DLP rule matching specified SITs.
claims.quote: New-DlpComplianceRule -Name "SocialSecurityRule" -Policy "USFinancialChecks" -ContentContainsSensitiveInformation @{Name="U.S. Social Security Number (SSN)"} -BlockAccess $True

claims.claim: The DLP cmdlet reference uses a hashtable that names the SIT.
claims.quote: For example, @(@{Name="U.S. Social Security Number (SSN)"; minCount="2"},@{Name="Credit Card Number"}).

claims.claim: The tenant's SIT inventory is under Microsoft Purview > Information Protection > Classifiers > Sensitive info types.
claims.quote: The Sensitive info types tab of the Classifiers page, lists all of the sensitive information types.

claims.claim: Get-DlpSensitiveInformationType lists the organization's SITs and -Identity "<SIT name>" retrieves a named SIT's properties.
claims.quote:
Get-DlpSensitiveInformationType -Identity "Credit Card Number" | Format-List

This example lists all the properties of the sensitive information type named "Credit Card Number".

claims.claim: RecommendedConfidence gives a SIT's default or recommended confidence level.
claims.quote: The RecommendedConfidence property of the returned objects contains a value that represents the default (or recommended) confidence level that should be used with the corresponding sensitive information type.

claims.claim: The SIT inventory operation is read-only rather than a setting.
claims.quote: Use the Get-DlpSensitiveInformationType cmdlet to list the sensitive information types that are defined for your organization in the Microsoft Purview compliance portal.

claims.claim: Copying SITs in the portal requires Purview role-group permissions.
claims.quote: The Microsoft Purview portal includes default role groups for tasks and functions for each compliance and governance solution that you need to assign people to.

claims.claim: Removing an individual custom SIT using PowerShell entails editing and re-importing its existing rule package.
claims.quote: Export the custom rule package containing the custom sensitive information type. Remove the sensitive information type from the XML file, and then import the updated XML file back into the existing custom rule package.

claims.claim: Remove-DlpSensitiveInformationTypeRulePackage -Identity "<rule package>" removes the specified custom rule package.
claims.quote: Remove-DlpSensitiveInformationTypeRulePackage -Identity "RulePackageIdentity"

claims.claim: Removing a custom rule package deletes all custom SITs it contains.

claims.where: Governance controls: Graph paragraph; Open questions
claims.claim: Microsoft Graph documents a sensitiveType resource under /beta/.
claims.quote: Represents information about a sensitive information type (SIT) used to classify content.

claims.claim: The sensitiveType resource is documented only under the beta Graph version.
claims.quote: Searched: "sensitiveType" "v1.0" Microsoft Graph. Read the sensitiveType beta resource reference (Methods: None) and Graph search results; no v1.0 sensitiveType resource reference found.

claims.claim: Sensitivity labels are a mechanism distinct from sensitive information type detectors.
claims.quote: DLP policies detect sensitive items by matching them to a sensitive information type (SIT), or to a sensitivity label or a retention label.

claims.claim: Custom SITs have a Publisher property value other than Microsoft Corporation.
claims.quote: For custom sensitive information types, the Publisher property value will be something other than "Microsoft Corporation".

claims.claim: The SIT instance count minimum supports 1 to 500.
claims.quote: The min field supports values of 1 to 500.

claims.claim: A numeric SIT instance count maximum supports 1 to 500.
claims.quote: Use a value between 1 and 500 when you want to set a specific upper limit of 500 or less on the number of instances of a SIT in an item.

claims.claim: The SIT instance count maximum also accepts Any.
claims.quote: Use Any when you want to ensure that the unique instance count criterion is satisfied when an undefined number of unique instances of a SIT are found in a scanned item

claims.where: Why it matters; Cost and licensing: supporting sources

claims.quote: When you select the Sensitive info types option, you see the same list of sensitive information types as when you create a data loss prevention (DLP) policy.
claims.fix: Add these two supporting pages to sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/purview/apply-sensitivity-label-automatically and https://learn.microsoft.com/office365/servicedescriptions/microsoft-365-service-descriptions/microsoft-365-tenantlevel-services-licensing-guidance/microsoft-purview-service-description. They support the labeling-action and solution-licensing statements; no additional product or licensing detail is needed.
